[[File:William Herrick Macaulay.jpg|thumb|right|William Herrick Macaulay, Vice-Provost, Kings College Cambridge]]
'''William Herrick Macaulay''' (16 November 1853 – 28 November 1936) was a [[People of the United Kingdom|British]] [[mathematician]], Fellow and Vice-Provost of [[King's College, Cambridge]], and close friend of [[Karl Pearson]].<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YFwckVLO-9UC&dq=%22herrick+macaulay%22&pg=PA181 | title=Karl Pearson: The Scientific Life in a Statistical Age | isbn=978-1-4008-3570-6 | last1=Porter | first1=Theodore M. | date=2 January 2010 | publisher=Princeton University Press }}</ref> He also corresponded with [[John Maynard Keynes]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://janus.lib.cam.ac.uk/db/node.xsp?id=CV%2FPers%2FMacaulay%2C%20William%20Herrick%20(1853-1936)%20mathematician |title=Macaulay William Herrick (1853-1936) mathematician |access-date=28 March 2013 |archive-date=23 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141023085007/http://janus.lib.cam.ac.uk/db/node.xsp?id=CV%2FPers%2FMacaulay%2C%20William%20Herrick%20(1853-1936)%20mathematician |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Family==
W. H. Macaulay was born in [[Hodnet, Shropshire]], in 1853, son of the Rev. Samuel Herrick Macaulay, rector of Hodnet and grandson of the Rev. [[Aulay Macaulay (writer)|Aulay Macaulay]]. His brothers included [[George Campbell Macaulay]], the father of Dame [[Rose Macaulay]], and [[Reginald Macaulay]]. He never married, and died in [[Clent]], near [[Stourbridge]], [[Worcestershire]], in 1936.<ref>[http://www.ukwhoswho.com/view/article/oupww/whowaswho/U213197 "MACAULAY, William Herrick,"] ''Who Was Who'', A & C Black Ltd., an imprint of Bloomsbury Publishing plc, 1920–2008; online edn, Oxford University Press, December 2007.</ref>

==Education, career and later life==
Unlike his elder brother (who went to [[Eton College|Eton]]), Macaulay was a pupil at [[Winchester College]]. Interested in the applied sciences rather than classics, upon leaving school he matriculated at [[Durham University]], where he was awarded both a B.A. degree and a prize fellowship in 1874. In October that year, he began a further degree in mathematics at [[King's College, Cambridge]], where he was made an Abbott Scholar and graduated as sixth [[Wrangler (Cambridge)|Wrangler]] at the [[University of Cambridge]] in 1878.<ref name="Venn">{{acad|FML874WH|name=William Herrick Macaulay}}</ref> 

Macaulay is best known for his work in [[Mechanical engineering|engineering]], most notably for his proposed [[Macaulay's method|mechanical technique]] in [[structural analysis]] for the purposes of beam or shaft deflection.{{citation needed|date=June 2020}} He was made a Fellow of King's in 1879, which was followed by further appointments as University Lecturer in mathematics in 1883 and as College Lecturer in applied mechanics a year later. He subsequently helped to establish the Department of Engineering at Cambridge.<ref name="Venn"/> He also worked for a time in a granite quarry.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pHPMpj2DedsC&q=%22herrick+macaulay%22&pg=PA123|title = Dissections: Plane and Fancy|isbn = 9780521525824|last1 = Frederickson|first1 = Greg N.|date = 3 February 2003| publisher=Cambridge University Press }}</ref>

Macaulay was appointed [[Bursar]] of King's in 1887, and following a decade-long role as Tutor in the college he became its Vice-Provost in 1918, remaining in post for six years until his retirement.<ref name="Venn"/> T. E. B. Howarth, in his book on inter-war Cambridge, remarked that Macaulay was "the last fellow [of King's] to follow the old practice of keeping a horse and riding regularly to hounds."<ref>T. E. B. Howarth, ''Cambridge Between Two Wars'' (London: Collins, 1978), p. 79. {{ISBN|0002111810}}</ref>
